title: Know the Way Out: Make a Home Fire Plan With a Friend
subtitle: A neighbor or friend can help turn an easy-to-postpone safety task into a clear, practiced plan—one made for the people and layout of each home.
imageAlt: Two friends sit at a kitchen table comparing separate hand-drawn home floor plans, with a clear doorway and window visible behind them.
imageConcept: Two male friends from different backgrounds sit together at a kitchen table, each marking exits on a separate simple floor plan; the mood is practical and companionable, with no emergency staged.
body:
A home fire escape plan is easy to put off because the work feels obvious: find a door, get outside. But smoke, confusion, a sleeping child or a route blocked by everyday clutter can make a familiar home feel different in an emergency. The U.S. Fire Administration says people may have less than two minutes to escape after a smoke alarm sounds. That is a reason to decide in advance, not to rush through a rehearsal or treat a sketch as a guarantee [1].

A friend can make the task easier to begin. Set aside an hour, bring paper and a pen, and work through each home separately. The goal is not to inspect or judge someone else’s space. It is to help one another notice details that are easy to miss when you move through the same rooms every day.
Start with the people who live there

Before drawing, list who needs to get out and what assistance might be needed. Include children, older adults, people with disabilities, anyone who may not hear an alarm, and visitors who stay overnight. If someone uses a mobility device or needs hands-on help, ask what works for them rather than making assumptions. A pet may need a plan too, but no one should re-enter a burning building to retrieve a person, animal or possession.

Agree on who will help whom, and on a backup if that person is away. For a child who stays between two homes, make a plan at both. For a roommate, be clear about who checks which room only if that can be done without delaying escape or entering danger. The plan should be understandable to everyone who needs to use it; add simple words or drawings if that helps.
Draw every room, then find the exits

Sketch the home’s rooms, hallways, doors and windows. The drawing does not need to be to scale; it needs to be legible. In each room, identify two ways out, as USFA recommends [1]. One may be a door and another a window, but only count a route that is actually usable and appropriate for that home. A window high above the ground, painted shut, or blocked by furniture is not a practical second way out just because it appears on paper.

Walk the routes together in daylight. Check how doors and windows open, whether screens or locks could slow someone down, and whether the path leads to a safe place outside. Do not improvise a route that involves an unsafe jump or climbing. If an exit is difficult to use, or the home’s layout makes two routes unclear, ask the property manager or local fire department for guidance rather than guessing.
Clear the routes you have chosen

A plan only works if the route remains passable. Notice shoes, laundry baskets, toys, charging cables, furniture and anything else that narrows a doorway or hallway. Move obstacles now, then agree on a simple way to keep those routes clear. If a door is normally locked, make sure household members know how it opens from inside. Check that a window identified as an exit can be opened by the person expected to use it.

For renters and people in multi-unit buildings, make the plan fit the building’s own instructions. A shared hallway, stairwell or exit may have rules that a hand-drawn household plan cannot override. Confirm the designated route with building management and follow posted directions. Do not use an exit that is blocked, unsafe or contrary to the building’s emergency guidance. The friend’s role is to help ask the right questions, not to certify the building.
Choose a meeting place everyone can find

Pick one outdoor meeting place a safe distance from the home, such as a particular tree or a neighbor’s front gate. Be specific: “outside” is not a location, and a large yard may leave people searching for one another. Put the meeting place on the drawing and make sure everyone in the household can identify it. If the usual spot could be inaccessible, agree on a backup.

Once outside, stay outside. Call emergency services from a safe location and tell responders if someone may still be inside. Do not go back in to search. The American Red Cross also advises households to identify two ways out of each room, choose an outdoor meeting spot, practice the plan twice a year and get out and stay out during a fire [2]. A friend can help make those decisions concrete, but the meeting place and roles need to work for the people who live there.
Practice without turning it into a scare

Walk the route at a calm time, with the people who will need to use it. Talk through what the alarm means, which exit each person will take and where everyone will meet. Practice at different times of day if that helps household members understand how the plan changes when someone is asleep or away. Keep the exercise low-pressure: no smoke, blindfolds, blocked doors or surprise alarms. Do not make anyone run or use an exit that has not been confirmed as safe.

Afterward, ask what felt confusing. Could everyone name the meeting point? Did a door stick? Was an instruction hard to hear or remember? Update the drawing and resolve practical problems. USFA recommends practicing with everyone in the home; practice is a chance to find a snag while there is time to fix it, not proof that every emergency will unfold as expected [1]. Repeat the walkthrough twice a year, and whenever the household or layout changes [2].
Check the alarms while you are there

A route plan and working alarms serve different purposes; check both. Test smoke alarms monthly, as the Consumer Product Safety Commission advises, and make sure people in the home know what their alarms sound like [3]. If an alarm does not work or its placement is uncertain, consult the manufacturer’s instructions, property manager or local fire department for next steps. Do not assume that a phone alert or a neighbor will substitute for an alarm inside the home.

This is also a sensible moment to notice nearby hazards without letting the walkthrough sprawl into a full home inspection. CPSC advises keeping portable heaters at least three feet from things that can burn and never operating a portable generator inside a home or other enclosed space [3]. Write down any concern that needs follow-up and assign a person and date to handle it. A short list that gets acted on is more useful than a long one that stays on the table.
Make the next visit the reminder

Before your friend leaves, take a photo of each finished plan and decide where it will be kept so household members can find it. Share a copy only with people who need it and are trusted with details about the home. Put a reminder on the calendar for the next twice-yearly practice, but treat the plan as something to revisit sooner if someone moves in, a child becomes more independent, a mobility need changes, or furniture alters a route.

On your next visit, ask one useful question: “Has anything changed that would make this plan harder to use?” Then walk the relevant route, update the drawing and confirm the meeting place again. This is not a promise that you can protect another household from every danger. It is a practical way to pay attention together—to make the exits visible, the responsibilities clear and the next step less likely to be left for someday.
